cemc-euclid-2003-01a.title: Use symmetry
cemc-euclid-2003-01a.body:
The $x$-intercepts are $2$ and $4$, so the axis of symmetry is $x = 3$.

Reflecting $(0, 8)$ in the line $x = 3$ gives $(6, 8)$, which is also on the parabola. Since $a \ne 0$, $a = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

cemc-euclid-2003-01a.title: Find the equation
cemc-euclid-2003-01a.body:
With roots $2$ and $4$, the parabola is $y = A(x-2)(x-4)$. Since $(0,8)$ is on it, $8 = 8A$, so $A = 1$ and $y = x^2 - 6x + 8$.

Setting $y = 8$: $x^2 - 6x = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 6$. Hence $a = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

cemc-euclid-2003-01b.title: Discriminant
cemc-euclid-2003-01b.body:
Equal roots means the discriminant is zero: $6^2 - 4(1)(k) = 0$, so $4k = 36$ and $k = 9$.

**Answer: 9**

cemc-euclid-2003-01b.title: Perfect square
cemc-euclid-2003-01b.body:
Equal roots means $x^2 + 6x + k$ is a perfect square, which must be $(x+3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9$. So $k = 9$.

**Answer: 9**

cemc-euclid-2003-01c.title: Find c, then intersect
cemc-euclid-2003-01c.body:
Since $(1,4)$ is on the parabola, $4 = 1 - 3 + c$, so $c = 6$.

Equate the line and the parabola:
$$x^2 - 3x + 6 = 2x + 2 \iff x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0 \iff (x-1)(x-4) = 0.$$
The new intersection has $x = 4$ and $y = 2(4) + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: $(4, 10)$**

cemc-euclid-2003-01c.title: Sum of roots
cemc-euclid-2003-01c.body:
After finding $c = 6$, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are the roots of $x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0$. Their sum is $5$, and one root is $1$, so the other is $4$. On the line, $y = 2\cdot 4 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: $(4, 10)$**

cemc-euclid-2003-02a.title: Solve for sin x
cemc-euclid-2003-02a.body:
$\sin x = \dfrac{\cos 15^\circ}{3} \approx \dfrac{0.96593}{3} \approx 0.32198$.

Since $x$ is acute, $x = \sin^{-1}(0.32198) \approx 18.78^\circ$, which is $18.8^\circ$ to the nearest tenth.

**Answer: $18.8^\circ$**

cemc-euclid-2003-02b.title: Use cosine
cemc-euclid-2003-02b.body:
$\cos C = \sqrt{1 - \frac{9}{25}} = \frac45$ (positive because $C$ is acute). Then $BC = AC\cos C = 20 \cdot \frac45 = 16$.

**Answer: 16**

cemc-euclid-2003-02c.title: Horizontal distances
cemc-euclid-2003-02c.body:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points on the ground directly below the helicopter at the two measurements and $G$ the goat.

- First: $\tan 6^\circ = \dfrac{222}{PG}$, so $PG = \dfrac{222}{\tan 6^\circ} \approx 2112.19$ m.
- Second: $\tan 75^\circ = \dfrac{222}{QG}$, so $QG = \dfrac{222}{\tan 75^\circ} \approx 59.48$ m.

In one minute the helicopter flies $2112.19 - 59.48 \approx 2052.71$ m $= 2.0527$ km. In one hour it flies $60 \times 2.0527 \approx 123.16$ km.

**Answer: about 123 km/h**

cemc-euclid-2003-02c.title: Use cotangents
cemc-euclid-2003-02c.body:
The horizontal distance from the goat when the angle of elevation is $\theta$ is $222\cot\theta$. So the distance flown in one minute is
$$222(\cot 6^\circ - \cot 75^\circ) \approx 222(9.5144 - 0.2679) \approx 2052.7\text{ m}.$$
Speed $= 2.0527 \text{ km/min} \times 60 \approx 123$ km/h.

**Answer: 123 km/h**

cemc-euclid-2003-03a.title: Shifted function
cemc-euclid-2003-03a.body:
Let $g(x) = f(x) + 3$. Then $g(2x+3) = f(2x+3) + 3 = 2f(x) + 6 = 2g(x)$.

Since $0 \to 3 \to 9$ under $x \mapsto 2x+3$, $g(9) = 4g(0) = 4 \cdot 9 = 36$, so $f(9) = 33$.

**Answer: 33**

cemc-euclid-2003-03b.title: Solve for f and g
cemc-euclid-2003-03b.body:
Halve the second equation: $f(x) + 2g(x) = x^2 + 2$. Subtracting from the first gives $g(x) = x + 4$, and then
$$f(x) = x^2 + 2 - 2(x+4) = x^2 - 2x - 6.$$
Now $f(x) = g(x)$ means $x^2 - 2x - 6 = x + 4$, i.e. $x^2 - 3x - 10 = 0$, i.e. $(x-5)(x+2) = 0$.

**Answer: $x = 5$ or $x = -2$**

cemc-euclid-2003-03b.title: Combine the equations directly
cemc-euclid-2003-03b.body:
Look for combinations of the equations:
$$(2f + 4g) - (f + 3g) = f + g, \qquad 2(f + 3g) - (2f + 4g) = 2g.$$
So $f + g = x^2 - x - 2$ and $2g = 2x + 8$. Then
$$f - g = (f + g) - 2g = x^2 - x - 2 - 2x - 8 = x^2 - 3x - 10 = (x-5)(x+2),$$
which is zero exactly when $x = 5$ or $x = -2$.

**Answer: $x = 5$ or $x = -2$**

cemc-euclid-2003-04a.title: Count finishing orders
cemc-euclid-2003-04a.body:
There are $5! = 120$ equally likely finishing orders. Neither Canadian medals exactly when the Canadians finish 4th and 5th: $2!$ ways for them and $3!$ ways for the other three, $12$ orders in all.

Probability $= \dfrac{12}{120} = \dfrac{1}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{10}$**

cemc-euclid-2003-04a.title: Who finishes last two
cemc-euclid-2003-04a.body:
The pair of skaters finishing 4th and 5th is equally likely to be any of the $\binom52 = 10$ pairs. Exactly one pair consists of the two Canadians, so the probability is $\frac{1}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{10}$**

cemc-euclid-2003-04b.title: Use a period of 30
cemc-euclid-2003-04b.body:
Whether a number has the property depends only on its remainder mod $\operatorname{lcm}(3,5,10,15) = 30$. From $1$ to $30$ the numbers that are multiples of 3 or 5 but not of 10 or 15 are
$$3, 5, 6, 9, 12, 18, 21, 24, 25, 27,$$
that is, $10$ numbers. The range $1$–$300$ consists of $10$ blocks of $30$, giving $10 \times 10 = 100$.

**Answer: 100**

cemc-euclid-2003-04b.title: Inclusion–exclusion
cemc-euclid-2003-04b.body:
- Multiples of 3 or 5: $100 + 60 - 20 = 140$.
- Remove the multiples of 15 (all $20$ of them are in the list): $120$ left.
- Remove the multiples of 10 that remain, i.e. multiples of 10 that are not multiples of 15 (not multiples of 30): $30 - 10 = 20$.

$120 - 20 = 100$.

**Answer: 100**

cemc-euclid-2003-05a.title: Groups of six
cemc-euclid-2003-05a.body:
The first six terms sum to $1 + 3 + 5 - 7 - 9 - 11 = -18$. In each later group of six, every term is $12$ larger in absolute value than the corresponding term of the previous group; three are added and three subtracted, so each group still sums to $-18$.

$300$ terms make $50$ groups, so the sum is $50(-18) = -900$.

**Answer: $-900$**

cemc-euclid-2003-05a.title: Pair terms
cemc-euclid-2003-05a.body:
Pair each positive term with the negative term three places later: $1 - 7$, $3 - 9$, $5 - 11$, $13 - 19$, ... Each pair equals $-6$. The $300$ terms form $150$ such pairs, so the sum is $150 \times (-6) = -900$.

**Answer: $-900$**

cemc-euclid-2003-05b.title: Factor the condition
cemc-euclid-2003-05b.body:
Let the tens digit be $a$ and the units digit $b$. Then
$$a^2 + 10b = b^2 + 10a \iff a^2 - b^2 - 10(a - b) = 0 \iff (a-b)(a+b-10) = 0.$$
So $a = b$ or $a + b = 10$. The candidates are
$11, 22, \ldots, 99$ and $19, 28, 37, 46, 55, 64, 73, 82, 91$.

Remove multiples of 11 other than 11 and even numbers: left with $11, 19, 37, 73, 91$. Since $91 = 7 \times 13$, the primes are $11, 19, 37, 73$.

**Answer: $11, 19, 37, 73$**

cemc-euclid-2003-06a.title: Count halvings
cemc-euclid-2003-06a.body:
In 24 minutes isotope A halves $4$ times, so its initial amount is $16$ times its amount at 24 minutes. Isotope B started with half as much, so its initial amount is $8 = 2^3$ times its amount at 24 minutes. So B halves 3 times in 24 minutes: once every 8 minutes.

**Answer: 8 minutes**

cemc-euclid-2003-06a.title: Equation
cemc-euclid-2003-06a.body:
Let the initial amounts be $2x$ and $x$, and let B's half-life be $T$. Then
$$2x\left(\tfrac12\right)^{24/6} = x\left(\tfrac12\right)^{24/T} \implies \left(\tfrac12\right)^3 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{24/T},$$
so $24/T = 3$ and $T = 8$.

**Answer: 8 minutes**

cemc-euclid-2003-06b.title: Linear system in the logs
cemc-euclid-2003-06b.body:
Both $x^3$ and $y^3$ must be positive, so $x, y > 0$. Let $X = \log_{10} x$ and $Y = \log_{10} y$. The equations become
$$3X + 2Y = 11, \qquad 2X - 3Y = 3.$$
Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2 and add: $13X = 39$, so $X = 3$. Then $2Y = 11 - 9 = 2$, so $Y = 1$.

Hence $x = 10^3 = 1000$ and $y = 10$.

**Answer: $x = 1000$, $y = 10$**

cemc-euclid-2003-06b.title: Exponential form
cemc-euclid-2003-06b.body:
The equations say $x^3y^2 = 10^{11}$ and $\dfrac{x^2}{y^3} = 10^3$. Cube the first and square the second: $x^9y^6 = 10^{33}$, $x^4y^{-6} = 10^6$. Multiply: $x^{13} = 10^{39}$, so $x = 10^3$.

Then $y^2 = 10^{11}/10^9 = 100$, so $y = \pm 10$; since $\log_{10}(y^3)$ needs $y > 0$, $y = 10$.

**Answer: $x = 1000$, $y = 10$**

cemc-euclid-2003-07a.title: Count equal triangles
cemc-euclid-2003-07a.body:
Let $U$ and $V$ be the two vertices of the inner hexagon nearest $A$ ($U$ on the side towards $F$). By symmetry the six small triangles such as $\triangle AUV$ between the hexagons are equilateral and congruent to the six triangles obtained by joining the centre $O$ of the inner hexagon to its vertices. Call the area of each of these $a$.

The remaining six regions, like $\triangle AUF$, also have area $a$: in $\triangle AFV$, $U$ is the midpoint of $FV$ (since $FU = UV$ by symmetry), so the median $AU$ splits it into two equal halves, $\triangle AUV$ and $\triangle AUF$.

So the big hexagon consists of $18$ pieces of area $a$, giving $a = 2$, and the inner hexagon has area $6a = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-euclid-2003-07a.title: Ratio of side lengths
cemc-euclid-2003-07a.body:
Let the inner hexagon have side $x$. The triangles at the outer vertices (e.g. at $A$) are equilateral with side $x$, and $\triangle AUF$ is isosceles with $AU = UF = x$ and apex angle $120^\circ$, so $AF = \sqrt3\,x$.

The hexagons are similar with side ratio $\sqrt3 : 1$, so area ratio $3 : 1$. The inner area is $36/3 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-euclid-2003-07b.title: Vertex form
cemc-euclid-2003-07b.body:
Put the cannon at $(0,0)$ with the $x$-axis pointing toward the net. The vertex is $(30, 100)$, so $y = a(x-30)^2 + 100$. Since $(0,0)$ is on it, $900a + 100 = 0$ and $a = -\frac19$.

Set $y = 64$: $(x - 30)^2 = 9 \cdot 36 = 324$, so $x - 30 = \pm 18$, i.e. $x = 12$ or $x = 48$. Herc is on his way down, past the vertex, so $x = 48$.

**Answer: 48 m**

cemc-euclid-2003-07b.title: Roots form
cemc-euclid-2003-07b.body:
The parabola is symmetric about $x = 30$ and has a root at $0$, so its other root is $60$: $y = ax(x - 60)$. At $x = 30$: $100 = -900a$, $a = -\frac19$.

$64 = -\frac19 x(x-60) \iff x^2 - 60x + 576 = 0 \iff (x-12)(x-48) = 0$. On the way down, $x = 48$.

**Answer: 48 m**

cemc-euclid-2003-08a.title: Coordinates
cemc-euclid-2003-08a.body:
Both the circle and $y = |x|$ are symmetric in the $y$-axis, so intersection points come in mirror pairs, except points on the $y$-axis. With exactly three intersection points, one lies on the $y$-axis; on $y = |x|$ that point is $O = (0,0)$.

Let the centre be $(0, b)$. Since $O$ is on the circle, the radius is $|b|$, and $b > 0$ (otherwise the circle lies below the $x$-axis except $O$ and meets $y=|x|$ only at $O$). The circle is $x^2 + (y-b)^2 = b^2$.

For $x \ge 0$, substitute $y = x$: $x^2 + (x - b)^2 = b^2 \iff 2x^2 - 2bx = 0 \iff x = 0$ or $x = b$. So $A = (b, b)$ and by symmetry $B = (-b, b)$.

Triangle $ABO$ has base $AB = 2b$ (on the line $y = b$) and height $b$, so its area is $\frac12(2b)(b) = b^2$. The circle has area $\pi b^2$. The ratio is $b^2 : \pi b^2 = 1 : \pi$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-08a.title: Synthetic
cemc-euclid-2003-08a.body:
Let $M$ be the centre and $r$ the radius; $O$ is on the circle and $MO$ lies along the $y$-axis, so $OM = r$ and the diameter from $O$ ends at $D = (0, 2r)$.

The chord $OA$ makes a $45^\circ$ angle with the diameter $OD$, so the inscribed angle at $O$ intercepts arc $AD$ of $90^\circ$; hence $\angle AMD = 90^\circ$, i.e. $MA$ is horizontal and $A = (r, r)$. Similarly $B = (-r, r)$, so $AB$ is a diameter and $\angle AOB = 90^\circ$ with $OA = OB = r\sqrt2$.

Area of $\triangle ABO = \frac12 (r\sqrt2)^2 = r^2$, and the circle's area is $\pi r^2$, giving $1 : \pi$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-08b.title: Congruent triangles and alternate angles
cemc-euclid-2003-08b.body:
$M$ is the midpoint of diameter $BC$, so it is the centre. $QP \perp PM$ (tangent ⟂ radius), and $QB \perp BM$ (right angle at $B$). Also $PM = BM$ (radii) and $QM$ is common, so $\triangle QPM \cong \triangle QBM$ (hypotenuse–side).

Let $\angle MQB = \angle MQP = \theta$. Then $\angle QMB = \angle QMP = 90^\circ - \theta$, and
$$\angle PMC = 180^\circ - 2(90^\circ - \theta) = 2\theta.$$
Triangle $PMC$ is isosceles ($PM = MC$), so $\angle MPC = \frac12(180^\circ - 2\theta) = 90^\circ - \theta = \angle PMQ$.

These are alternate angles for the lines $QM$ and $AC$ with transversal $PM$, so $QM \parallel AC$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-08b.title: Q is the midpoint of AB
cemc-euclid-2003-08b.body:
Join $PB$. Since $BC$ is a diameter, $\angle BPC = 90^\circ$, so $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.

Let $\angle PCB = x$. By the tangent–chord theorem $\angle QPB = x$, so $\angle APQ = 90^\circ - x$. In right triangle $ABC$, $\angle PAQ = 90^\circ - x$. Thus $\triangle AQP$ is isosceles with $AQ = QP$.

$QB$ is also tangent to the circle (it is perpendicular to the radius $MB$), so $QP = QB$ (equal tangents). Hence $AQ = QB$: $Q$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Since $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, the midsegment theorem in $\triangle ABC$ gives $QM \parallel AC$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-09.title: Cosine law twice
cemc-euclid-2003-09.body:
Let $x = \cos\angle ABC = CD$ (so $x > 0$) and $y = BC$. In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles are supplementary, so
$$\cos\angle ADC = -x, \qquad \cos\angle BCD = -\cos\angle BAD = \tfrac13.$$

Compute $AC^2$ in two ways:
- $\triangle ABC$: $AC^2 = 1 + y^2 - 2y\,x$.
- $\triangle ADC$: $AC^2 = 1 + x^2 - 2x(-x) = 1 + 3x^2$.

So $y^2 - 2xy - 3x^2 = 0$, i.e. $(y - 3x)(y + x) = 0$. Since $x, y > 0$, $y = 3x$.

Now in $\triangle BCD$, with $CD = x$, $BC = 3x$, $\cos\angle BCD = \frac13$:
$$BD^2 = x^2 + 9x^2 - 2(x)(3x)\cdot\tfrac13 = 8x^2.$$
Then $BD^2 + CD^2 = 9x^2 = BC^2$, so $\angle BDC = 90^\circ$. An inscribed right angle subtends a diameter, so $BC$ is a diameter. ∎

(For completeness: in $\triangle ABD$, $BD^2 = 1 + 1 + \frac23 = \frac83$, so $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $BC = \sqrt3$; such a quadrilateral really exists.)

cemc-euclid-2003-09.title: Projection view
cemc-euclid-2003-09.body:
As above, the cosine law for $AC$ in triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ gives $BC = 3\,CD$.

Drop the perpendicular from $B$ to line $CD$, meeting it at $H$. Then $CH = BC\cos\angle BCD = 3\,CD \cdot \frac13 = CD$, and $H$ lies on ray $CD$ because $\angle BCD$ is acute. So $H = D$, meaning $BD \perp CD$ and $\angle BDC = 90^\circ$. By the converse of Thales' theorem, $BC$ is a diameter. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-10a.title: Build the partition
cemc-euclid-2003-10a.body:
$1 + 2 + \cdots + 8 = 36$, so each set must sum to $12$. $C$ must contain $3$ and $6$ (sum $9$), so it needs $3$ more from non-multiples of 3. $A \subseteq \{1, 5, 7\}$, $B \subseteq \{2, 4, 8\}$.

Take $A = \{5, 7\}$ (sum 12), $B = \{4, 8\}$ (sum 12), and $C = \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$ (sum 12). All conditions hold, so 8 is savage. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-10b.title: Case analysis on n mod 6
cemc-euclid-2003-10b.body:
Each number that is not a multiple of 3 is either in $C$, or (if odd) in $A$, or (if even) in $B$. Let $S = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$; each set must sum to $S/3$. Write $\Sigma X$ for the sum of set $X$. Since $n$ is even, $n = 6k$, $6k+2$ or $6k+4$.

**$n = 6k$.** Split $1, \ldots, 6k$ into triples $(1,2,3), (4,5,6), \ldots$. $C$ contains the largest number of each triple, so $\Sigma C > \frac13 S$. Impossible.

**$n = 6k+4$.** $S = (3k+2)(6k+5) = 18k^2 + 27k + 10 = 3(6k^2 + 9k + 3) + 1$ is not divisible by 3. Impossible.

**$n = 6k+2$.** $S = (3k+1)(6k+3)$, so the target is $T = (3k+1)(2k+1) = 6k^2 + 5k + 1$.

- $C \supseteq \{3, 6, \ldots, 6k\}$, whose sum is $3 \cdot \frac{2k(2k+1)}{2} = 6k^2 + 3k$.
- The odd non-multiples of 3 up to $n$ sum to $(1 + 3 + \cdots + (6k+1)) - (3 + 9 + \cdots + (6k-3)) = (3k+1)^2 - 3k^2 = 6k^2 + 6k + 1 = T + k$.
- The even non-multiples of 3 up to $n$ sum to $(2 + 4 + \cdots + (6k+2)) - (6 + 12 + \cdots + 6k) = (3k+1)(3k+2) - 3k(k+1) = 6k^2 + 6k + 2 = T + (k+1)$.

$B$ consists of the even non-multiples of 3 except those placed in $C$. For $\Sigma B = T$, the even numbers moved to $C$ must total $k + 1$. A sum of even numbers is even, so $k + 1$ is even and $k = 2l + 1$. Then $n = 6(2l+1) + 2 = 12l + 8$ and
$$\frac{n+4}{12} = l + 1$$
is an integer. ∎

cemc-euclid-2003-10c.title: Check the candidates from (b)
cemc-euclid-2003-10c.body:
By (b), $n = 12l + 8$, i.e. $n = 6k + 2$ with $k$ odd: $n \in \{8, 20, 32, 44, 56, 68, 80, 92\}$ with $k = 1, 3, 5, \ldots, 15$.

From the computation in (b), starting with all multiples of 3 in $C$, all other odd numbers in $A$ and all other even numbers in $B$, we must move odd non-multiples of 3 with total $k$ from $A$ to $C$, and even non-multiples of 3 with total $k + 1$ from $B$ to $C$ (and this is also sufficient). The available odd numbers are $1, 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots$ and even numbers $2, 4, 8, 10, 14, \ldots$.

| $n$ | $k$ | remove from $A$ | remove from $B$ | possible? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 1 | 1: $\{1\}$ | 2: $\{2\}$ | yes |
| 20 | 3 | 3 | 4 | no: no odd non-multiples of 3 sum to 3 |
| 32 | 5 | 5: $\{5\}$ | 6: $\{2, 4\}$ | yes |
| 44 | 7 | 7: $\{7\}$ | 8: $\{8\}$ | yes |
| 56 | 9 | 9 | 10 | no: from $\{1, 5, 7\}$ no subset sums to 9 |
| 68 | 11 | 11: $\{11\}$ | 12: $\{4, 8\}$ | yes |
| 80 | 13 | 13: $\{13\}$ | 14: $\{14\}$ | yes |
| 92 | 15 | 15 | 16 | no: from $\{1, 5, 7, 11, 13\}$ no subset sums to 15 |

For $k = 15$: an odd total needs an odd number of odd terms; one term would be $15$ (a multiple of 3), and the smallest three are $1 + 5 + 7 = 13$, next $1 + 5 + 11 = 17 > 15$, so none works.

**Answer: $8, 32, 44, 68, 80$**
